title: How does Java classloading work (Bootstrap → Platform → Application loaders, delegation model), and can two classes with the same fully-qualified name coexist in one JVM (yes — if loaded by different classloaders, as in app servers/plugins)?
shortTitle: How does Java classloading work, and can two classes with the same name coexist in one JVM?

s1_definition.profdef: Java classloading is the process by which the JVM finds, loads, links, and initializes class definitions on demand at run time. It is performed by a hierarchy of class loaders: the Bootstrap loader loads the core platform classes, the Platform loader loads other standard JDK modules, and the Application (system) loader loads your application's classpath or module path. They cooperate through the parent-delegation model, where a loader first asks its parent to load a class and only loads it itself if the parent cannot. A class's identity in the JVM is its fully-qualified name combined with the class loader that defined it, which means two classes with the same name can coexist in one JVM if they are loaded by different class loaders, which is exactly how application servers and plugin systems isolate deployments.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of class loaders as a chain of librarians at National Bank of India. When a clerk requests a document, the junior librarian does not grab it immediately; he first asks his senior, who asks the chief librarian, and only if the seniors do not have it does the request come back down for the junior to fetch his own copy. This parent-delegation keeps the one true copy of core documents at the top, so everyone shares the same official policy manual. But here is the subtle part: the bank identifies a document not just by its title but by which librarian issued it. So two documents titled "Fee Policy" issued by two different departmental librarians are treated as two genuinely different documents, which is how the bank runs two versions of a plugin side by side without them clashing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Class loaders form a delegating hierarchy, Bootstrap then Platform then Application, and a class's identity is its name plus its loader, so the same class name loaded by different loaders yields distinct, coexisting classes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Java classloading is the process by which the JVM finds, loads, links, and initializes class definitions on demand at run time. It is performed by a hierarchy of class loaders: the Bootstrap loader loads the core platform classes, the Platform loader loads other standard JDK modules, and the Application (system) loader loads your application's classpath or module path. They cooperate through the parent-delegation model, where a loader first asks its parent to load a class and only loads it itself if the parent cannot. A class's identity in the JVM is its fully-qualified name combined with the class loader that defined it, which means two classes with the same name can coexist in one JVM if they are loaded by different class loaders, which is exactly how application servers and plugin systems isolate deployments.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of class loaders as a chain of librarians at National Bank of India. When a clerk requests a document, the junior librarian does not grab it immediately; he first asks his senior, who asks the chief librarian, and only if the seniors do not have it does the request come back down for the junior to fetch his own copy. This parent-delegation keeps the one true copy of core documents at the top, so everyone shares the same official policy manual. But here is the subtle part: the bank identifies a document not just by its title but by which librarian issued it. So two documents titled "Fee Policy" issued by two different departmental librarians are treated as two genuinely different documents, which is how the bank runs two versions of a plugin side by side without them clashing.

**One line to remember:** Class loaders form a delegating hierarchy, Bootstrap then Platform then Application, and a class's identity is its name plus its loader, so the same class name loaded by different loaders yields distinct, coexisting classes.

sections.s2_technical:
Classloading happens lazily: the JVM loads a class the first time it is actively used, for example when you create an instance, call a static method, or access a static field. The lifecycle has three stages. Loading finds the class's bytes and creates a `Class` object. Linking has three substeps: verification checks the bytecode is valid and safe, preparation allocates static fields with default values, and resolution turns symbolic references into direct references. Initialization runs the static initializers and static field assignments, exactly once, in a thread-safe way guaranteed by the JVM.

The loaders form a hierarchy. The Bootstrap class loader is the root, written in native code, and it loads the core classes like those in `java.base`, including `java.lang.Object` and `String`. It is represented as `null` when you ask a class for its loader, because it is not a Java object. Below it is the Platform class loader, which in the modular JDK loads the other standard platform modules that are not part of the bootstrap set. Below that is the Application or system class loader, which loads classes from your application's classpath or module path; this is the loader returned by `ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader()` and the one that loads your `main` class.

The parent-delegation model governs how they cooperate. When a loader is asked to load a class, it first delegates to its parent, and only if every ancestor fails to find the class does the loader attempt to load it itself. This has two important effects. First, core classes are always loaded by the Bootstrap loader, so you can never accidentally replace `java.lang.String` with your own version on the classpath, which is a security guarantee. Second, it avoids duplicate loading of shared classes, because a class the parent can load is loaded once by the parent and shared downward. The standard method flow is that `loadClass` checks if the class is already loaded, then delegates to the parent, then calls `findClass` to load it locally if the parent failed.

Now the identity rule, which is the crux of the second half of the question. In the JVM a class is uniquely identified not by its fully-qualified name alone but by the pair of its name and the class loader that defined it, called its defining loader. This pair is sometimes called the runtime package or the class's run-time identity. The consequence is that if two different class loaders each load a class named `com.bank.FeePolicy`, the JVM treats them as two distinct classes. They have separate `Class` objects, separate static fields, and are not assignment-compatible: assigning an instance of one to a variable typed by the other throws `ClassCastException`, even though the source code and bytes are identical. This is why you sometimes see the confusing error that a `FeePolicy` cannot be cast to a `FeePolicy`, the two being from different loaders.

This identity rule is not a bug; it is the foundation of isolation. Application servers like Tomcat and JBoss give each deployed web application its own class loader, so two applications can bundle different versions of the same library without conflict, and so one application's classes are invisible to another. This deliberately breaks strict parent-delegation: a web app class loader often checks its own war first for application classes before delegating, so each app sees its own bundled version, while still delegating to the parent for core and server classes. Plugin and modular systems like OSGi do the same, giving each bundle a loader with carefully controlled visibility, which lets you load, unload, and even hot-swap different versions of a module at run time. When a class loader and all its classes and instances become unreachable, the whole loader can be garbage-collected, which is how undeploying an application frees its classes.

A senior nuance: this power is also a source of leaks. If something outside a web app, such as a thread-local, a cache, or a JDBC driver registered in a parent, holds a reference to a class or instance from the app's loader, the loader cannot be collected on undeploy, and you get a class-loader leak that slowly exhausts metaspace across redeployments. Diagnosing these is a classic production task. Understanding that identity equals name plus loader is the key to both using isolation deliberately and debugging when it goes wrong.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a plugin platform where different business units supply their own `FeePolicy` implementation jar, and two units happen to ship a class with the exact same fully-qualified name but different logic. On a single flat classpath they would clash and one would shadow the other. This is exactly the different-class-loaders case: give each plugin its own class loader so both `FeePolicy` classes coexist as distinct classes.

Problem 2 — The platform must guarantee that core classes like the shared `Account` type come from one authoritative source and cannot be overridden by a plugin. This is the parent-delegation case: the shared types are loaded by the parent loader and delegated down, so every plugin sees the same `Account`.

Problem 3 — A developer was confused by a `ClassCastException` that said a `FeePolicy` could not be cast to a `FeePolicy`. This is the identity-equals-name-plus-loader case: two same-named classes from different loaders are genuinely different types.

The mini-project builds a tiny plugin loader. We create two child class loaders, each loading its own version of a fee-policy class from a separate location, and show that the two loaded classes are distinct, that each computes fees differently for Rajesh and Priya, and that casting across loaders fails.

The code contains: a `PluginClassLoader`; a demo that loads the same class name through two loaders; and proof they are distinct classes.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the host app
javac -d out $(find src/main/java -name "*.java")

# Compile the two plugin versions into separate directories (same fq-name!)
mkdir -p plugins/a plugins/b
javac -d plugins/a PluginAFeePolicy.java   # returns Rs.50.00
javac -d plugins/b PluginBFeePolicy.java   # returns Rs.75.00

# Run — both FeePolicy classes coexist in one JVM via distinct loaders
java -cp out com.bank.plugin.ClassLoaderDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a request to load two plugins that each define a class named `com.bank.ext.FeePolicy`, then compute fees for Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1: We print the hierarchy. The application loader's parent is the Platform loader, whose parent is Bootstrap, shown as null. This is the chain every normal class load delegates up.

Step 2: We create two `PluginClassLoader` instances, A and B, each with the application loader as parent but pointing at a different plugin directory.

Step 3: `Class.forName("com.bank.ext.FeePolicy", true, loaderA)`. Loader A first delegates to its parent to load `FeePolicy`. The parent cannot find it on the app classpath, so delegation fails upward, and loader A's `findClass` reads the bytes from plugins/a and defines the class. Its identity is now `FeePolicy` plus loader A.

Step 4: The same call through loader B defines a second `FeePolicy` from plugins/b, with identity `FeePolicy` plus loader B.

Step 5: We compare `feeA == feeB`, which is false. Same name, different loaders, so two distinct `Class` objects coexist in the one JVM.

Step 6: We instantiate each and invoke `feeFor` reflectively. Plugin A returns Rs.50.00 for Rajesh's SAV2001; plugin B returns Rs.75.00 for Priya's CUR3001. Both run side by side without clashing.

Step 7: If we tried to cast a plugin B instance to the plugin A class, the JVM would throw `ClassCastException` because they are genuinely different types, which is the identity rule made visible.

```

    │ 1. already loaded? no
    │ 2. delegate ↑ to parent (App → Platform → Bootstrap)
    │        parents cannot find it → fail upward
    │ 3. findClass locally → read plugins/a/.../FeePolicy.class → defineClass
    ▼
  Class object = (name "com.bank.ext.FeePolicy" , loader plugin-a)

  loadClass same name on loaderB
    │ delegate ↑ fails → findClass → plugins/b → defineClass
    ▼
  Class object = (name "com.bank.ext.FeePolicy" , loader plugin-b)

  feeA == feeB ?  ──→ FALSE  (identity = name + loader)
    │
    ├─ policyA.feeFor("SAV2001") → Rs.50.00   (Rajesh, plugin A logic)
    ├─ policyB.feeFor("CUR3001") → Rs.75.00   (Priya, plugin B logic)
    └─ cast B-instance to A-class → ClassCastException (distinct types)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Java classloading is how the JVM finds, loads, links, and initializes classes on demand at run time, and it is done by a hierarchy of class loaders. The Bootstrap loader, written in native code and shown as null, loads the core platform classes like Object and String. The Platform loader loads the other standard JDK modules. The Application or system loader loads my application's classpath or module path, including my main class. They cooperate through the parent-delegation model: when a loader is asked for a class, it first delegates to its parent, and only if every ancestor fails does it load the class itself. This guarantees that core classes always come from the Bootstrap loader, so I can never replace java.lang.String with my own, and it avoids duplicate loading of shared classes.

The crux of the second part is the identity rule. In the JVM a class is identified not by its fully-qualified name alone but by the pair of its name and the class loader that defined it. So yes, two classes with the same fully-qualified name can absolutely coexist in one JVM, as long as they are loaded by different class loaders. They get separate Class objects, separate static fields, and are not assignment-compatible, which is why you sometimes see the confusing error that a FeePolicy cannot be cast to a FeePolicy, the two coming from different loaders.

This is not a quirk; it is the foundation of isolation. Application servers like Tomcat give each deployed web application its own class loader so two applications can bundle different versions of the same library without conflict, and plugin systems like OSGi do the same to load, unload, and hot-swap module versions. In my work at National Bank of India I used exactly this for a plugin platform where two business units shipped a fee-policy class with the identical name but different logic. I gave each plugin its own child class loader, so both classes coexisted as distinct types, each computing fees its own way, while the shared core types were loaded once by the parent and delegated down. The senior point I always add is that this power is also a leak risk: if something outside an application, like a thread-local, a cache, or a driver registered in a parent, holds a reference into the application's loader, that loader cannot be garbage-collected on undeploy, and you get a class-loader leak that slowly exhausts metaspace, which is a classic production problem to diagnose.
